title: Host-symbiont bleaching dynamics under thermal stress
headline: THREE OF THE FOUR INTERVENTIONS BUY A CORAL THAT STILL LOOKS BROWN WHILE IT STARVES. Measured on two readouts: on symbiont loss all four design knobs move the failure threshold by a comparable amount, but on the host's CARBON BALANCE the symbiont thermal optimum moves it 5.9 times further than the next best knob (+2.00 degC of anomaly against +0.34, +0.28 and +0.21). Raising photoprotection, ROS tolerance or symbiont retention keeps the ALGAE IN PLACE without keeping the HOST FED. Anyone selecting on visual bleaching score -- which is most of the restoration field -- is scoring the readout that cannot tell those apart. And the thermal knob is not free either. With the trade-off Cunning et al. measured put into the model -- heat-tolerant symbiont proportion raises bleaching resistance and lowers photochemical efficiency, linearly -- the thermal gain from +2 degC falls to zero at a coupling strength of 0.39 -- but whether a real coral sits before or after that point cannot be answered here, because the measured 29% growth penalty is NOT REACHABLE as a steady state at any coupling in the swept range: the worst the model will produce is -14.4%, and past that the holobiont drops into the bleached alternate state instead of settling at a larger penalty. A second arm reaches the same gap by scaling the carbon-fixation ceiling directly, so it is the model's bistability and not either arm's parameterisation. Underneath all of it: the dynamical core is a line-by-line port of the published coRal model, reproducing the author's own R code to 5e-15 relative error, but CORAL HAS NO TEMPERATURE IN IT -- the published model bleaches corals with light. The thermal coupling is this file's addition, it enters through exactly one parameter, and every thermal number here is a property of that extension. The unmodified holobiont bleaches at 5.7 degree heating weeks, which is where the single calibrated parameter put it and is therefore not evidence about NOAA's 4-8 window.

provenance.code: results/coral/code/bleaching_dynamics.py (with coral_deb.py and coral_reference_run.R beside it)

model_source.name: coRal
model_source.paper: Cunning R, Muller EB, Gates RD, Nisbet RM (2017) J Theor Biol 431:49-62
model_source.note: The equations and all 23 of its parameter values were taken from the code, which was read. The PAPER was not obtained; its abstract is the only part read. Where this file quotes a reason for a parameter value, the quote is from a comment in def_pars.R, not from the paper.

model.name: coRal (ported) + one thermal coupling
model.kind: deterministic ODE system, explicit Euler, biomass-specific DEB

state_variables.name: S/H
state_variables.meaning: symbiont-to-host ratio; THIS is the quantity that reaches a steady state. Measured here by running the unmodified R code over a 4x5 light-by-DIN grid: H and S themselves grow or shrink exponentially without bound, because the model is biomass-specific and has no size limit. Every readout is defined on the ratio.

model.causal_chain: light absorbed per symbiont carbon (jL, self-shaded by S/H) -> carbon fixed (jCP, capped by jCPm and divided by the current ROS factor) -> excess excitation energy (jeL = jL - jCP/yCL) -> what NPQ cannot dissipate (jeL - jNPQ, with jNPQ saturating at kNPQ) -> ROS factor (cROS = 1 + ((jeL-jNPQ)/kROS)^k) -> symbiont turnover (jST = jST0(1 + b(cROS-1))) -> symbiont loss. Every step is Cunning et al.'s. Temperature enters at exactly one place: jCPm -> jCPm*phi(T).

thermal_extension.equation: jCPm_effective(T) = jCPm * exp(-0.5*((T-T_opt)/sigma)^2), sigma = sigma_hot above T_opt and sigma_cold below
thermal_extension.why_this_term: Warner, Fitt & Schmidt 1999 (PMID 10393938, abstract): heat damages the PSII D1 protein faster than it is replaced, and the authors state that perturbation of PSII protein turnover during photoinhibition at elevated temperature underlies symbiont collapse. A falling ceiling on photochemistry is what that is in this model's accounting.
thermal_extension.scope_of_the_negative: No temperature term appears in any source file of the cloned coRal repository. A case-insensitive search of the whole tree (excluding .git) for 'temp', 'thermal', 'heat', 'degC' and 'dhw' returns exactly ONE match, and it is not a temperature term: `.Rbuildignore:2:^\.Rproj\.user$  # used for temporary files.` -- an incidental hit on 'temporary' inside a build-ignore comment. POSITIVE CONTROLS for the same search: 'symbiont' matches 14 files, 'light' 14, 'photo' 12, 'carbon' 9, so the search runs and finds what is there. This is a statement about the CODE as published at commit 7c90f9be, not about the paper, which was not read in full.

parameters.name: L_control
parameters.source: Constant downwelling irradiance for every arm. Held CONSTANT rather than seasonal so that the degree-heating-week threshold is attributable to temperature alone: coRal drives bleaching with light, so a seasonal light cycle in phase with the seasonal temperature cycle would confound the two. A seasonal-light arm is run as a robustness check and reported separately. 30 mol photons m^-2 d^-1 is a shallow tropical reef order of magnitude; no measurement was retrieved.

parameters.name: N_control
parameters.source: External dissolved inorganic nitrogen, 1 uM. coRal's own documented example uses 1e-7, which in this port gives a host whose specific growth rate is negative (measured: dH/Hdt < 0 at L >= 10). 1e-6 puts the control in positive energy balance. No reef measurement was retrieved; this is a model-operating choice.

parameters.name: X_control
parameters.source: No heterotrophic feeding in any arm, so autotrophy is the only carbon source and the bleaching response is not cushioned by feeding. Cunning et al.'s own abstract states bleaching is 'attenuated by feeding', so this is the conservative, bleaching-prone choice.

parameters.name: MMM
parameters.source: Maximum monthly mean used as the DHW reference. A representative tropical value; NOT a site measurement and not taken from any climatology file. Only differences from it matter to the result.

parameters.name: seasonal_amplitude
parameters.source: Half-range of the annual sea-temperature cycle. Representative; no published value used.

parameters.name: T_opt
parameters.source: Thermal optimum of symbiont photochemistry in the added performance curve. No published value applies across Symbiodiniaceae genera. This is the baseline the sweep moves away from; the SPAN carries the meaning, not the value.

parameters.name: sigma_hot
parameters.source: Width of the thermal performance curve above the optimum. THIS IS THE ONE CALIBRATED PARAMETER: it was chosen so the unmodified holobiont bleaches inside the NOAA 4-8 degree-heating-week window. A model calibrated to that window cannot then be used as evidence about it, and nothing here claims it is.

parameters.name: tradeoff_kappa
parameters.units: fractional loss of photochemical efficiency per degC of thermal optimum
parameters.source: THE STRUCTURE IS SOURCED AND THE MAGNITUDE IS NOT. Cunning, Silverstein & Baker 2015 (PMID 26041354, abstract) report that in Orbicella faveolata 'higher proportions of heat-tolerant symbionts LINEARLY increased bleaching resistance but REDUCED PHOTOCHEMICAL EFFICIENCY'. So the thermal knob is not free: it is bought against the symbiont's capacity to turn absorbed light into fixed carbon. This file encodes it on jCPm, the maximum specific photosynthate production rate: jCPm_effective = jCPm * phi(T) * (1 - kappa * (T_opt - 28)). THE FIRST ENCODING WAS ON yCL AND CAME OUT WITH THE WRONG SIGN, which is recorded because it is a trap in coRal's photon accounting rather than a typo: excess excitation energy is jeL = jL - jCP/yCL, so LOWERING the quantum yield makes each unit of fixed carbon consume more photons, which REDUCES the excess and therefore reduces ROS. Measured, with the coupling on yCL: raising kappa from 0 to 0.3 IMPROVED both the thermal gain (+2.000 to +2.137 degC) and the ambient cost (-1.65% to -0.10%) -- the trade-off made the coral better, which is not what the source says. On jCPm the direction is the intended one: a lower ceiling on carbon fixation leaves more absorbed light unused AND delivers less carbon to the host. The LINEARITY and the SIGN come from that sentence; kappa itself does not, because the abstract gives no slope, so kappa is SWEPT rather than set and the default of 0 is the uncoupled model. NOTE THE SPECIES: Orbicella faveolata is a massive Caribbean coral, not an Acropora, so applying this coupling to an Acropora route is a cross-genus assumption.

parameters.name: sigma_cold
parameters.source: Width below the optimum, set wider than sigma_hot because thermal performance curves of photosynthetic organisms are left-skewed. Not fitted to anything.

parameters.name: dhw_hotspot_offset
parameters.source: NOAA Coral Reef Watch convention: HotSpots are summed into degree heating weeks only when SST exceeds the maximum monthly mean by at least 1 degC. Source read: the NOAA CRW DHW product page (coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/product/5km/tutorial/crw10a_dhw_product.php), read_level web-page. The primary methods papers (Liu et al.; Glynn & D'Croz 1990; Eakin et al. 2010) were NOT retrieved and are not cited.

parameters.name: dhw_window
parameters.source: NOAA CRW: DHW is the running sum of HotSpots over the previous 12 weeks. Same page, read_level web-page.

parameters.name: DHW_alert1
parameters.source: NOAA CRW: at 4 degC-weeks 'you can expect to see coral bleaching reef-wide, especially in more sensitive coral species'. Same page, read_level web-page. Note the page as summarised does not itself label 4 and 8 as Alert Levels 1 and 2.

parameters.name: DHW_alert2
parameters.source: NOAA CRW: at 8 degC-weeks 'you are likely to see reef-wide coral bleaching with mortality of heat-sensitive corals'. Same page.

parameters.name: DHW_realism_ceiling
parameters.source: Thresholds above this are reported as 'beyond observed forcing' rather than as numbers. Twice NOAA's mortality level. A declared reporting cut, not a biological quantity.

parameters.name: bleaching_criterion
parameters.source: DECLARED BEFORE THE SWEEP. Bleaching is the symbiont-to-host ratio falling below half its control steady-state value. Chosen because visible paling corresponds to a large fractional symbiont loss; no study used 0.5 as a cut. The sensitivity of every conclusion to this number is reported (criterion_sensitivity).

parameters.name: spinup_years
parameters.source: Ambient run before any anomaly, so the heatwave acts on a settled symbiosis. Checked: the control passes its stationarity conditions.

parameters.name: anomaly_max
parameters.source: Peak of the thermal anomaly in the standard forcing. Large enough that even the most tolerant corner of the knob map bleaches or is reported censored; larger than any single observed reef anomaly.

parameters.name: sustain_days
parameters.source: A readout condition must hold for this long before it counts as a crossing. DECLARED BEFORE THE SWEEP. coRal's initialisation resets the flux variables whatever the biomass state, so every run begins with a one-step transient; requiring persistence makes every readout immune to it and to any other brief excursion. Two weeks is a round number.

parameters.name: anomaly_ramp
parameters.source: The anomaly rises linearly over this many days, so degree heating weeks accumulate smoothly and the DHW at first bleaching is well resolved rather than jumping between time steps.

T_opt.route: Durusdinium trenchii shuffling or inoculation; heat-evolved strains
T_opt.range_basis: SOURCED SPAN. Berkelmans & van Oppen 2006 (PMID 16928632) report about +1 to +1.5 degC from a C-to-D shift in Acropora millepora; Pettay et al. 2015 (PMID 26034268) report +1 to +2 degC for Durusdinium trenchii in Caribbean hosts. A 2 degC span is the top of the measured range for the symbiont-identity route. Both read at abstract level.

kNPQ.route: Photoprotective pigments; the SS8 heat-evolved strain's reported mechanism
kNPQ.range_basis: ASSUMED SPAN, a doubling. Chan et al. 2023 (PMID 37913765, abstract) report that in SS8-hosting Galaxea fascicularis 'algal pigments involved in photobiology and oxidative stress were the greatest contributors to the thermotolerance differences', but no study gives a factor by which NPQ capacity can be raised. A doubling is a round number, not a measured ceiling.

kROS.route: Symbiont and host ROS handling; antioxidant frontloading
kROS.range_basis: ASSUMED SPAN, a doubling. Buerger et al. 2020 (PMID 32426508, read at FULL TEXT) measured wild-type Symbiodiniaceae secreting '~13- to 28-fold higher' extracellular ROS than heat-evolved strains after three weeks at 31 degC. That is NOT this parameter: kROS is the excess excitation energy at which ROS production doubles, not a secreted ROS concentration, and the two cannot be converted into one another. The doubling used here is therefore assumed and is far more conservative than a 13-28x difference in a different quantity would suggest.

b.route: Host regulation of symbiont expulsion; HSF1 and antioxidant frontloading
b.range_basis: ASSUMED SPAN, a halving of the coRal default, chosen to match the other two multiplicative knobs so the ranges are at least comparable in kind. jST = jST0*(1 + b*(cROS-1)), so b sets how strongly oxidative stress converts into symbiont loss. Barshis et al. 2013 (PMID 23297204, abstract) show resilient Acropora hyacinthus colonies constitutively 'frontload' antioxidant and heat-shock transcripts, but nothing measures the resulting change in b. The direction is from the biology; the magnitude is invented.

readouts.control_steady_state: mean S/H over the final year of a 3-year ambient run

readout_A_bleaching.definition: S/H below 0.5 of the control steady state; DECLARED BEFORE THE SWEEP. Threshold = NOAA degree heating weeks accumulated at that moment.
confound_source_lines: coRal R/def_pars.R:43:    b=rep(5, nsym)  # Scaling parameter for bleaching response
readout_A_bleaching.confound: NOT independent of the knob b. The two lines above are the whole of it: jST = jST0*(1 + b*(cROS-1)) is the only equation in which symbiont loss is produced, and b is its coefficient, so a knob acting on expulsion necessarily dominates a readout defined as expulsion. Measured: at the retentive end of b's range this readout censors most of the knob map, because a host that does not expel symbionts never crosses the criterion at any dose. That is close to tautological and is why readout B exists.

readout_B_host_energy.definition: Degree heating weeks at which the host's specific growth rate dH/Hdt first goes negative, i.e. translocated photosynthate no longer covers maintenance.
readout_B_host_energy.why: b does not appear in the host growth equation, so this readout is not confounded with any knob. It also asks a different question: not 'did the coral pale' but 'did the symbiosis stop paying for itself'. A holobiont that retains ROS-damaged symbionts scores as unbleached on readout A and can still fail on readout B. The additivity verdict is taken on THIS readout.

readout_C_ambient_cost.definition: Mean host specific growth rate over the fourth year of a purely ambient run, relative to the wild type.
readout_C_ambient_cost.why: The cost side. Every thermal-tolerance route is scored for what it gives up when there is no heatwave, which is the half of the symbiont literature a thermal-threshold model otherwise silently ignores.

port_check.reference_run: R 4.3.3, coRal R/run_coral.R with def_pars() unchanged, dt=0.1 d, 365 days, three environments
port_check.note: With the thermal extension OFF, this port must reproduce the published R code exactly. This is the positive control for the whole study: a port that silently diverged would look exactly like a model with different biology in it.

step_halving.criterion: relative change in the wild-type threshold below 0.05, DECLARED BEFORE THE RUN
step_halving.reported_as_failed_not_relaxed: This check FAILS and the criterion was not moved. coRal integrates with explicit Euler and so does this port; a first-order scheme converges slowly, and a first-crossing readout inherits that error directly. The convergence table below quantifies it, the Richardson estimate gives the limit, and the ranking check shows which conclusions survive. The absolute threshold does not survive; the knob ranking and the additivity verdict do.

convergence.note: Readout A (degree heating weeks at symbiont loss) is still moving at the smallest step tried; the Richardson estimate of its limit is given and the quoted threshold should be read as carrying that much discretisation uncertainty on top of everything else. Readout B in degC of anomaly is much better behaved because the anomaly is a smooth monotone function of time with no 1 degC deadband.

ranking_vs_step_size.note: The absolute threshold is not converged; this asks whether the ORDER of the four knobs is, which is what the design question needs.

criterion_sensitivity.note: Declared criterion is 0.5. The threshold moves with it, as it must; what matters for the design question is whether the RANKING of knobs moves, which is tested separately.

ranking_robustness.note: Span in threshold DHW across each knob's declared range, recomputed under two other bleaching criteria and under a seasonal light field. A knob ordering that survives all three is a property of the model; one that does not is a property of the readout.

degree_heating_weeks_blind_spot.finding: Degree heating weeks cannot see a sub-1-degC failure, by construction.
degree_heating_weeks_blind_spot.why: NOAA Coral Reef Watch sums HotSpots into degree heating weeks only where sea temperature exceeds the maximum monthly mean by at least 1 degC. Any failure mode that bites below that accumulates exactly zero DHW, however severe it is.
degree_heating_weeks_blind_spot.measured_here: The wild-type holobiont's carbon balance goes negative at an anomaly of about 0.75 degC -- right at the deadband -- where the DHW reading is still 0.00. In three of the four knob panels the host-energy threshold sits at or near zero degree heating weeks for the whole sweep, not because nothing happens but because the metric cannot register it.
degree_heating_weeks_blind_spot.consequence: Anyone using degree heating weeks as a design currency, or as the trigger for an intervention, is blind to this mode. It is a property of the metric and not of the model, and it is why the knob ranking and the additivity verdict in this study are taken in degC of anomaly rather than in degC-weeks.

emergent_cold_arm.interpretation: Emergent, not fitted. The model bleaches on cooling as well as on warming, because both lower carbon fixation and so raise excess excitation energy. This has the same SIGN as the cold bleaching reported by Silverstein et al. 2017 in C3-hosting Montastraea cavernosa, which is a weak consistency check and not a validation: no magnitude here was compared to theirs, and DHW has no cold analogue so no threshold is reported.

emergent_ambient_cost.finding: Raising the symbiont thermal optimum by 2 degC changes the host's ambient specific growth rate by -1.65%. It is the only knob of the four whose ambient effect is negative; the other three improve ambient growth, because they all reduce the oxidative burden the control is already carrying (control cROS = 1.215, i.e. ROS production is already above baseline at ambient in this model).
emergent_ambient_cost.interpretation: Nothing was tuned for this. The mechanism is that a symbiont whose optimum sits above the ambient range is below its optimum for most of the year, fixes less carbon, and therefore leaves more absorbed light unused. That is the right SIGN for the measured Durusdinium trade-off (Jones & Berkelmans 2010: 29% slower in the laboratory, 38% in the field) and about an order of magnitude too small. So this model does NOT support a shifted thermal optimum as the explanation of that penalty, which is a finding about the model and a pointer to the alternatives the literature already offers: reduced carbon translocation per cell (Sproles et al. 2020, in an anemone) or something not in the model at all. Kemp et al. 2023 (PMID 37727091) report no ambient nutrient-exchange difference between Cladocopium and Durusdinium colonies, so the measured cost is itself disputed and the model is not adjudicating it.

durusdinium_cost_arm.finding: Reducing the symbiont's carbon-fixation ceiling drives host growth down continuously only as far as -22.3%, at jCPm multiplier 0.44; below that the holobiont falls into the bleached state with negative host growth. There is NO steady state in this model with the 29-38% growth penalty Jones & Berkelmans measured. Either the model's alternate-stable-state transition is too abrupt, or the measured Durusdinium penalty is not a carbon-fixation-ceiling effect and some other term carries it. The model cannot tell which, and does not claim to.

tradeoff_arm.verdict: THE TWO CANNOT BE COMPARED ON THIS AXIS, and that is the finding. The measured 29% ambient growth penalty is NOT REACHABLE as a steady state at any coupling strength in the swept range: the worst steady-state cost the model will produce is -14.4%, and beyond that the holobiont falls into the bleached alternate state with negative host growth rather than settling at a larger penalty. That is the same gap the Durusdinium cost arm finds by a completely different route -- scaling the carbon-fixation ceiling directly rather than coupling it to the thermal optimum -- so it is a property of the model's bistability and not of either arm's parameterisation. Either this model's alternate-stable-state transition is too abrupt, or the measured Durusdinium penalty is not a carbon-fixation effect at all.
tradeoff_arm.coupling: yCL_effective = yCL * (1 - kappa * (T_opt - 28 degC)), floored at 0.05

coupling_structure_source.cite: Cunning, Silverstein & Baker 2015, Proc Biol Sci 282:20141725
coupling_structure_source.quote: higher proportions of heat-tolerant symbionts linearly increased bleaching resistance but reduced photochemical efficiency
coupling_structure_source.cross_genus_note: Orbicella faveolata is a massive Caribbean coral. Most of the rest of this design space is Acropora-centred, so applying this coupling to an Acropora route is a cross-genus assumption and is flagged as one.

cost_target_source.quote: type D corals grew 29% slower in the laboratory and 38% slower in the field than C2-hosting colonies

tradeoff_arm.caveat: Two different studies, two different genera, one model. The coupling's structure is from Orbicella and the cost target is from Acropora, and the model is not evidence that they belong on the same axis. What it can do is show what WOULD follow if they did.

sweeps.saturation_note: Readout A saturates: for three of the four knobs the modified end of the range does not fail until the forcing ramp itself runs out, so the span measured on readout A is a property of the +4 degC cap and not of the knob. Those points are flagged at_forcing_cap and are excluded from the additivity fit. Readout B does not saturate, which is the second reason the ranking is taken there.
sweeps.ranking_caveat: The four declared ranges are not commensurable: 2 degC of thermal optimum against two doublings against a fivefold cut. The span therefore measures the range as much as the knob. The elasticity block is the commensurable comparison.

additivity.readout_meaning: anomaly in degC at which host specific growth first goes negative and stays negative; NOT confounded with the knob b, and free of the 1 degC deadband that degree heating weeks carry by construction
additivity.exclusion_rule: Cells that never crossed (censored) and cells that crossed only within two time steps of the top of the forcing ramp (at the forcing cap) are BOTH excluded. A cap crossing is the forcing running out, not a measured threshold, and including it would pile a spurious plateau into the fit.
additivity.verdict_rule: DECLARED BEFORE THE FIT: additive if two-way terms add < 0.02 adjusted R^2.

additivity_on_symbiont_readout.readout_meaning: degree heating weeks at which S/H falls below the declared bleaching criterion; CONFOUNDED with the knob b, which is the coefficient converting oxidative stress into symbiont loss
additivity_on_symbiont_readout.exclusion_rule: Cells that never crossed (censored) and cells that crossed only within two time steps of the top of the forcing ramp (at the forcing cap) are BOTH excluded. A cap crossing is the forcing running out, not a measured threshold, and including it would pile a spurious plateau into the fit.
additivity_on_symbiont_readout.verdict_rule: DECLARED BEFORE THE FIT: additive if two-way terms add < 0.02 adjusted R^2.

answer_to_the_design_question.question: Are the thermal-tolerance knobs additive, or does one dominate?
answer_to_the_design_question.answer: In this model, over these ranges, on the readout that is not confounded with any knob (host carbon balance): additive. Main effects alone reach adjusted R2 0.999 on the 2401 usable cells of the 2401-cell map, and all six two-way interactions together add 0.001. Ranked by span: T_opt (+2.00 degC of anomaly), kROS (+0.34 degC of anomaly), kNPQ (+0.28 degC of anomaly), b (+0.21 degC of anomaly).
answer_to_the_design_question.the_result_the_two_readouts_disagree_abo: On readout A (symbiont loss) all four knobs move the threshold by a comparable amount. On readout B (host carbon balance) T_opt moves it about six times further than any of the other three. Read together: raising photoprotection, ROS tolerance or symbiont retention mostly keeps the ALGAE IN PLACE without keeping the HOST FED, whereas moving the symbiont's thermal optimum delays both. In this model, three of the four interventions buy a coral that still looks brown while it starves. That is a statement about a model whose host has no food source but its symbiont, and it is the kind of thing a single-readout study would not see at all.
answer_to_the_design_question.why_two_readouts: The obvious readout -- degree heating weeks at which the coral loses half its symbionts -- cannot answer this question cleanly, because one of the four knobs (b) is the coefficient that converts oxidative stress into symbiont loss. Asking whether b dominates a symbiont-loss readout is close to asking whether b equals b. Measured: on that readout 1868 of 2401 map cells are censored because retentive hosts never cross the criterion at any dose. The host-energy readout has no such relationship to any knob, and the verdict is taken there. Both are reported.
answer_to_the_design_question.caveat: 'Additive' here is a property of a four-parameter box in one model. It is not a claim that two real interventions combine additively in a coral, which nobody has tested: no study in the research block crosses a symbiont swap with a host trait.

limitations: This is a SIMULATION. No coral was measured. Nothing here is evidence that any intervention raises a real coral's bleaching threshold.

coRal CONTAINS NO TEMPERATURE. The published model bleaches corals with light, not heat. The thermal coupling is this file's addition, it enters through exactly one parameter, and every number that depends on temperature depends on that choice. A different coupling -- heat acting on symbiont growth, on host respiration, or on the repair arm directly -- would give different thresholds.

ONE parameter was calibrated: sigma_hot, set so the unmodified holobiont bleaches inside the observed 4-8 degree-heating-week window. The model therefore cannot be used as evidence about that window, and the headline says so.

The thermal performance curve is an assumed shape with three assumed parameters. No measured thermal performance curve for Symbiodiniaceae photochemistry was retrieved; the research block records that symbiont density per cm2, a bleached-density threshold, mitotic index and absolute Fv/Fm are all unavailable from the sources read.

The knob RANGES are three-quarters invented. Only T_opt's 2 degC span is sourced (Berkelmans & van Oppen 2006; Pettay et al. 2015, both abstracts). The two doublings and the fivefold cut in b are round numbers. So the ranking of knobs by span is partly a ranking of my choices, which is why the elasticity block exists.

Host and symbiont biomass are unbounded in coRal, so 'the colony died' is not representable: the model has no mortality. A holobiont whose S/H collapses is scored as bleached, and what happens to it afterwards is outside the model.

One symbiont type, not a population. Symbiont shuffling -- the route that most of the symbiont literature is about -- is a change in the MIX of two or more types, and cannot be represented by moving one thermal optimum. coRal supports multiple symbionts (nsym > 1) and this port does not use that; a shuffling study would.
No acclimatisation and no plasticity: the knobs are constants in time, so the preconditioning route (Ainsworth et al. 2016) cannot be represented at all. Nor can anything epigenetic.

The growth cost IS scored (readout C), but it comes out about an order of magnitude too small. Raising the thermal optimum by 2 degC costs under 2% of host specific growth here, against the 29% (laboratory) and 38% (field) that Jones & Berkelmans 2010 measured for Durusdinium-hosting Acropora millepora, and the 'nearly half' calcification reduction Pettay et al. 2015 report. The Durusdinium cost arm shows the model has no steady state with a penalty that large at all. So the model reproduces the SIGN of the trade-off and not its size, and nothing here should be read as a prediction of what a symbiont swap costs.

Calcification is not in the model at all. coRal tracks host carbon biomass, not skeleton, so the Pettay 'nearly half' calcification figure has no counterpart here and the comparison above is to GROWTH, which is a different quantity measured a different way.

Light is constant in the main arms and the anomaly is a single linear ramp. Real thermal histories are not ramps, and in coRal light is the primary driver, so a reef whose summer light and summer temperature peak together is a harsher case than anything here. The seasonal-light robustness arm is one step toward that and not a substitute for real forcing.

DEGREE HEATING WEEKS CANNOT SEE A SUB-1-degC FAILURE, by construction. The NOAA convention sums HotSpots only where SST exceeds the maximum monthly mean by at least 1 degC, so any failure mode that bites below that accumulates zero DHW. In this model host carbon balance is exactly such a mode: the wild type's growth rate goes negative at an anomaly of about +1 degC, right at the deadband, where the DHW reading is still 0. That is why readout B is reported in degC of anomaly as well, and why the knob ranking and the additivity verdict are taken in degC rather than in degC-weeks. It is a property of the metric, not of the model, and it is worth knowing for anything that uses DHW as a design currency.

The host is fragile here BECAUSE feeding was switched off. X = 0 in every arm, so the host has no carbon source but its symbiont. Cunning et al.'s own abstract states that bleaching in this model is 'attenuated by feeding', so a fed holobiont would fail later and readout B's sensitivity is partly a consequence of a declared modelling choice.

Degree heating weeks are computed to the NOAA convention from a SYNTHETIC temperature series. The 4 and 8 degC-week lines on the figures are field thresholds drawn for scale, taken from the NOAA product page at read_level web-page; the primary methods papers were not obtained.

The bleaching criterion (0.5 of control S/H) is declared but arbitrary. Thresholds move with it, as the criterion_sensitivity block shows. What is tested is whether the knob RANKING moves, which is a weaker claim than it sounds: it is still a ranking inside one model.
